title: Aligos Therapeutics Announces the Completion of Enrollment in the Phase 2 B-SUPREME Study of Pevifoscorvir Sodium Under Development for the Treatment of Chronic HBV Infection

analysis.time: Publication date: 2026-07-13. Event date: Not reported in the supplied evidence. Study timeline: Enrollment completed. topline safety and efficacy data expected in late Q3 2027.
analysis.location_and_population: Global, with study sites unspecified. Participants: 131 HBeAg+ adults and 114 HBeAg- adults with chronic HBV infection.
analysis.event: Aligos Therapeutics announced completion of enrollment in the Phase 2 B-SUPREME study of pevifoscorvir sodium for chronic HBV infection. This is a company-reported, ongoing clinical trial.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: Total enrolled: 245 adults (131 HBeAg+ and 114 HBeAg-). No cases, deaths, or exposures reported as this is a clinical trial enrollment update. Primary endpoints include HBV DNA suppression. No risk level stated.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: second interim analysis waived due to over-enrollment. Topline results expected late Q3 2027. No treatment, prevention, or public health response actions reported. Uncertainty: efficacy and safety data pending.

analysis.brief_en: Aligos Therapeutics announced the global completion of enrollment in its Phase 2 B-SUPREME study of pevifoscorvir sodium for chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection. The trial enrolled 245 adults split between HBeAg-positive (131) and HBeAg-negative (114) groups across international sites. The randomized, double-blind study compares pevifoscorvir sodium monotherapy to tenofovir disoproxil fumarate over 48 weeks, with primary endpoints assessing HBV DNA suppression. Topline safety and efficacy data are anticipated in late Q3 2027. The investigational oral capsid assembly modulator has shown promising antiviral activity in earlier trials.

title: Study reveals mechanism underlying HBV-induced liver inflammation

analysis.time: Publication date: 17 July 2026. Event date: Not reported in the supplied evidence.
analysis.location_and_population: Research conducted at Chongqing Medical University, China. validated in HBV transgenic mice and pAAV/HBV1.2 mouse models. Human liver samples from patients with chronic HBV infection were analyzed.
analysis.event: A mechanistic study published in Genes & Diseases identified a ROS-dependent signaling cascade that activates the Jak2/Stat3 pathway, triggering hepatic inflammatory responses in chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection. The event is reported as a scientific finding, not an outbreak or public-health incident.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: No cases, deaths, or exposures were reported. The study describes molecular mechanisms underlying HBV-induced liver inflammation and identifies ROS-dependent Jak2/Stat3 activation as a potential therapeutic target.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The study is preliminary and mechanistic, based on transcriptomic analyses, cell-line experiments, and mouse models. Further validation in clinical settings and human trials is required. The source is a reputable scientific news outlet summarizing peer-reviewed research.

analysis.brief_en: A study published on 17 July 2026 by researchers at Chongqing Medical University reveals a molecular mechanism linking chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection to liver inflammation. The team found that HBV replication disrupts mitochondrial function, causing excessive reactive oxygen species (ROS) accumulation that activates the Jak2/Stat3 inflammatory pathway via Nrf2-regulated cytokines IL-6 and IL-8. Experiments in HBV transgenic mice and patient liver samples confirmed this ROS-dependent cascade, while antioxidant treatment (NAC) reduced inflammation. The findings identify ROS-driven Jak2/Stat3 signaling as a potential therapeutic target to prevent inflammation-driven liver disease progression in chronic HBV patients.
analysis.summary_en: A study published on 17 July 2026 by researchers at Chongqing Medical University reveals a molecular mechanism linking chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection to liver inflammation. The team found that HBV replication disrupts mitochondrial function, causing excessive reactive oxygen species (ROS) accumulation that activates the Jak2/Stat3 inflammatory pathway via Nrf2-regulated cytokines IL-6 and IL-8. Experiments in HBV transgenic mice and patient liver samples confirmed this ROS-dependent cascade, while antioxidant treatment (NAC) reduced inflammation. The findings identify ROS-driven Jak2/Stat3 signaling as a potential therapeutic target to prevent inflammation-driven liver disease progression in chronic HBV patients.

title: Coroner raises concerns over lack of national guidance on prescribing for hepatitis B reactivation - The Pharmaceutical Journal

analysis.time: The event occurred on 12 September 2025, with the coroner's report published on 10 July 2026 and the response sent on 6 July 2026.
analysis.location_and_population: The event took place in Inner London North, UK, involving a 41-year-old patient with a renal transplant and chronic hepatitis B.
analysis.event: A coroner raised concerns over the lack of national guidance on prescribing and monitoring for hepatitis B reactivation, following the death of a patient who died from complications due to the inadvertent discontinuation of necessary medical treatment.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The patient died from complications of hepatitis B reactivation. The coroner noted a lack of national guidance and specialized commissioning for hepatitis B services, which could pose a risk to other patients.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The coroner directed concerns to the British Viral Hepatitis Group and the UK Health Security Agency. The British Association for the Study of the Liver (BASL) responded that it does not lead the development of clinical guidelines, and that monitoring and prescribing responsibilities vary between NHS trusts.

analysis.brief_en: A coroner in Inner London North, UK, has raised concerns over the lack of national guidance on prescribing and monitoring for hepatitis B reactivation, following the death of a 41-year-old patient with a renal transplant and chronic hepatitis B. The patient died on 12 September 2025 from complications due to the inadvertent discontinuation of necessary medical treatment. The coroner's report, published on 10 July 2026, highlighted that the patient's medication was discontinued in early 2025, leading to hepatitis B reactivation. The coroner directed concerns to the British Viral Hepatitis Group and the UK Health Security Agency, noting a lack of specialized commissioning for hepatitis B services. The British Association for the Study of the Liver (BASL) responded that it does not lead the development of clinical guidelines and that responsibilities vary between NHS trusts.

title: Hepatitis B Vaccination Crucial for Guinea-Bissau: Ethicist - Medscape

analysis.time: Publication date: 2026-07-17. Event date: Not reported in the supplied evidence. The commentary discusses a proposed study and its suspension, but no specific event date is provided.
analysis.location_and_population: Guinea-Bissau, a low-income country in West Africa. Affected population: newborns and children. The commentary also references the United States in the context of policy discussions.
analysis.event: A medical ethicist (Arthur L. Caplan, PhD) publicly criticized a proposed unethical study in Guinea-Bissau that would test hepatitis B vaccination efficacy using a placebo control in 15,000 children. The study was suspended but not definitively canceled. The ethicist argues hepatitis B vaccination is essential and already proven safe and effective.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: Not reported in the supplied evidence. The commentary does not provide case counts, death counts, or current disease burden data for Guinea-Bissau. The proposed study involved 15,000 children, but no outcomes or risks are detailed.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The proposed study has been suspended but not definitively canceled. The CDC has paused the study following criticism. The ethicist and others advocate for immediate vaccination programs in Guinea-Bissau instead of further study. No official prevention, testing, or treatment actions are reported beyond the suspension.

analysis.brief_en: A New York University medical ethicist has condemned a proposed unethical study in Guinea-Bissau that aimed to test hepatitis B vaccination efficacy using a placebo control in 15,000 children. Arthur L. Caplan, PhD, argued the vaccine is already proven safe and effective, and the study design exploited poverty in one of the world’s poorest nations. The study has been suspended but not definitively canceled, and the ethicist called for immediate vaccination programs instead. The commentary highlights ongoing debates over hepatitis B vaccination policies in the U.S. and globally.

title: Health Bureau monitors 23,000 hepatitis B patients - The Macau Post Daily

analysis.time: Publication date: 2026-07-14. Event date: 2026-07-13 (press conference). Time range: February 2025 onward for screening expansion. July 25, 2026 for rapid testing event.
analysis.location_and_population: Macau (Macao SAR, China), including residents aged 40 and above without prior HBsAg testing, and individuals aged 50 or above with no testing record. Community associations and public health facilities involved.
analysis.event: Macau Health Bureau (SSM) reported ongoing monitoring of approximately 23,000 chronic hepatitis B patients under medical management. The event is confirmed and involves public health guidance and screening initiatives.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: About 23,000 chronic hepatitis B patients under monitoring. Estimated 34,000 infected residents in Macau (2016 data). HBsAg positivity rate: 7.6% among adults aged 18+ (moderate prevalence). Children under 5: 0.03% positivity rate (meets WHO standard ≤0.1%). Hepatitis B positivity rate among residents born in the 1990s: ~2%. No acute outbreak or surge reported.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: SSM expanded HBsAg testing to residents aged 40+ without prior testing (since June 2026) and previously to those aged 50+ (since February 2025).
